Training Data
Machine learning models learn from a set of labeled data during a 
training phase. This data consists of input-output pairs, allowing 
the model to understand patterns and relationships.
Learning Algorithms
ML algorithms are the mathematical models that enable machines 
to learn. These algorithms use the training data to identify 
patterns, make predictions, or classify new, unseen data.
Features and Labels
In supervised learning, the input variables are called features, and 
the output variable to be predicted is called the label. The model 
learns the mapping between features and labels during training.

Types of Supervised Learning
Supervised learning encompasses regression for continuous outcomes and 
classification for discrete outcomes, including algorithms such as linear 
regression, decision trees, and neural networks.
Linear Regression
• For predicting continuous values based on linear relationships between 
input features and the target variable.
Logistic Regression
• For binary classification tasks, where the output variable has two classes.
Decision Trees, Random Forests
• For both classification and regression tasks, decision trees partition the 
feature space into regions and make predictions based on majority voting or 
averaging.
Support Vector Machines (SVM)
• For binary classification tasks, SVM finds the optimal hyperplane that 
separates classes in the feature space.

Types of Unsupervised Learning
Unsupervised learning includes clustering for grouping similar data points and 
association rule mining for discovering relationships among variables.
K-Means Clustering
• A partitioning algorithm that divides data points into K clusters 
based on similarity.
Hierarchical Clustering
• Builds a hierarchy of clusters by recursively merging or splitting 
clusters based on their similarity.
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
• Reduces the dimensionality of the dataset by projecting it onto a 
lower-dimensional subspace while retaining most of the variance.

Solving The Water-Jug Problem
The Water-Jug Problem stands as a quintessential challenge in the domain of
Artificial Intelligence (AI), amenable to resolution through diverse search
algorithms. Breadth-First Search (BFS) offers a systematic approach to
tackle this problem, adhering to the following principles.
State Representation: Each state encapsulates the 
water volume in each jug at a given step.
Initial State: Commences with one jug at full 
capacity and the other empty.
Possible Actions:
Filling a jug to its full capacity.
Completely emptying a jug.
Transferring water from one jug to another 
until either the recipient jug is full or the 
source jug is empty.
BFS Exploration: Systematically investigates all 
potential actions from the initial state and 
successive resultant states.
Goal State: Attains fulfilment upon reaching a 
state where one jug contains the target water 
volume.
© Aptech Limited 11
The N-Queen Problem
The N-Queens problem epitomizes a fundamental challenge in AI, frequently 
tackled through the application of the backtracking algorithm. 
Problem Statement
Place N queens on an N x N chessboard, ensuring that no queen threatens another 
along diagonals, rows, or columns. Here is the backtracking algorithm:
Begin by situating a queen in the first column, iterating through each row.
Recursively endeavor to place queens in subsequent columns.
In each column, verify if a queen can be positioned securely in any accessible 
row.
Upon discovering a safe placement, advance to the next column and repeat the 
process.
If no secure placement is possible in a column (backtracking), remove the queen 
from the previous column and try a different row for placement.

Introduction to Knowledge 
Representation
Knowledge Representation is a fundamental concept in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cognitive science. It refers to the process of
encoding knowledge in a form that a computer system can interpret and utilize to reason, make decisions, or perform tasks. Here
is a detailed description:
Concept Knowledge representation transforms real-world knowledge into a computer-readable format, 
crucial for decision-making. It encompasses factual and procedural information.
Importance Effective knowledge representation is pivotal for AI, underpinning reasoning, problem-
solving, and decision-making. It enables AI systems to interpret data, draw conclusions, and 
make informed actions.
Approaches Various approaches to knowledge representation exist, such as logical representation, 
semantic networks, frames, and production rules. Each method provides distinct ways of 
organizing and utilizing information.
Techniques Logical representation utilizes symbols and rules to represent knowledge, while semantic 
networks organize information with nodes and edges. Frames structure knowledge into units, 
and production rules encode knowledge through conditional statements.
Examples Examples of knowledge representation encompass medical knowledge for diagnosis, financial 
data for investment decisions, and linguistic knowledge for natural language processing.

Query Process in Knowledge Representation
In knowledge representation systems, processing a query involves several steps to
retrieve relevant information or infer new knowledge.
Feedback and Iteration: The user can provide feedback on the query results, which can be used to refine the query or improve the 
knowledge representation model. 
Result Generation: Finally, the results of the query execution are generated and presented to a user in a structured format. This can 
include returning relevant facts, entities, or relationships that match the query criteria, along with any derived knowledge or inferred 
conclusions. 
Query Execution: Once the query has been processed and relevant information identified, it is executed against the knowledge base. 
Inference and Reasoning: Inference mechanisms are applied to the query to derive new knowledge or infer relationships based on the 
existing knowledge base. 
Semantic Mapping: Once parsed, the query is mapped to the underlying knowledge representation model. 
Parsing the Query: The query is initially parsed to break it down into its constituent parts, such as keywords, entities, relationships, 
and constraints.

Propositional and Predicate Logic
Propositional Logic
• Propositional logic, or sentential logic, handles 
true/false statements using logical operators.
• Syntax: Propositions are symbolized (for 
example., p, q), and operators include AND, 
OR, NOT, IF-THEN, IF, AND ONLY IF.
• Semantics: Truth values are assigned based on 
constituent parts and logical operators' 
meanings.
• Example: With p as 'It is raining' and q as 'The 
streets are wet', 'It is raining AND the streets 
are wet' is p AND q.
Predicate Logic
• Predicate logic, or first-order logic, expands 
propositional logic with predicates, variables, 
quantifiers, and functions, offering more 
nuanced representations of object relationships.
• Syntax: Predicates denote properties or 
relations (for example., P(x), Q(x, y)), variables 
signify objects and quantifiers (∀, ∃) determine 
variable scope.
• Semantics: Predicate logic semantics define 
predicate interpretations and truth assignments 
to quantified statements.
• Example: With P(x) as 'x is prime' and Q(x, y) 
as 'x is the parent of y', ∀x ∃y Q(x, y) denotes 
'each person x has a child y'.
Propositional logic operates on true or false propositions using logical operators such as AND, OR,
and NOT, while predicate logic extends this to handle relationships and quantified statements with
variables and predicates.

Data Representation Through Propositional 
and Predicate Logic
Propositional Logic
• Propositional logic represents data as atomic
propositions that can be either true or false.
• It deals with simple relationships and
constraints using logical operators such as
AND, OR, NOT, IF-THEN, and IF AND
ONLYIF.
• Data is represented as individual propositions
or logical combinations of propositions,
allowing machines to reason about the truth
values of statements.
• For example, in a smart home system,
propositions such as ‘The lights are on’ or ‘The
door is locked’ can be represented using
propositional logic.
Predicate Logic
• Predicate logic extends propositional logic by
introducing predicates, variables, quantifiers, and
functions, enabling the representation of more complex
relationships and properties of objects.
• Data is represented using predicates to express
properties or relations between objects, variables to
denote objects in the domain, and quantifiers to specify
the scope of variables.
• Predicate logic allows for the representation of
quantified statements, such as ‘For every person x,
there exists a person y such that x is the parent of y’.
• In AI applications, predicate logic is used to represent
knowledge about the world in a more expressive and
flexible manner, enabling machines to reason about
objects, relationships, and constraints.
Representing data to machines through propositional and predicate logic is
fundamental in Artificial Intelligence (AI) for capturing and processing information
in a structured and logical manner.
